# **Chapter 1: Introduction**

## **1.1 Chapter Overview**

This chapter highlights our project, what it is used for, who uses it and how it can benefit us and our users

## **1.2 Client and/or Project Brief**

## This project is focused on helping the government and local communities to prevent floods. We came up with this project to help save flood victims and other people who are in flood-risk zones. We used the feedback from our feedback sessions and supervision sessions as pointers to what the people who we want to help would need. 

## **1.3 Problem Background**

## In countries like Sri Lanka, there is a high risk of flood. Floods can occur frequently or at certain intervals. When floods occur a lot of people are affected and it requires a significant amount of financial resources to be able to recover the damages. However, with the use of our DrainWatch we can ensure that people are alerted of the incoming flood ahead of time and they can take precautionary measures to reduce the financial resources used to recover the damage later. This can also reduce the loss of life that will occur in the case of a regular flood. As there have been recent floods in places like Germany, Afghanistan, Indonesia and some others as well, within a few years ago (FloodList, 2024). 

## **1.4 Problem Statement**

## *“Flooding can cause a lot of damage”*

## 

## **1.5 Proposed Solution**

## By using sensors on drains and rivers that are close to civilizations, we can monitor water levels. We place two sensors at certain levels in the rivers and drains, and when the water level reaches the first sensor, a notification is sent to alert the local residents of a rise in water levels. If the water levels reach the second sensor then an alarm goes off user devices to alert a wider range of residents to take evacuation measures to avoid incoming floods 

## **1.6 Aim**

## *“To save as many people from floods”*

Our project looks to ensure more lives are not lost to floods and to take preventive measures to protect all residents who are at risk of floods. 

## **1.7 Project Scope**

### **1.7.1 In-scope**

Create a notification alert component in the system as well as an alarm alert. A section for residents to upload their own claims of rising water levels at areas with no sensors or in case of sensor malfunction. A heat map generated by user inputs and sensors to show areas where increases in water levels are more frequent.

### **1.7.2 Out-scope**

Flood forecasting will not be implemented in our system. We will only be focusing on preventing floods by monitoring water levels, not predicting the future.

## **2.2 Competitor Analysis**

### **2.2.1 Competitor Introduction**

Google Flood Hub is a competitor within this space. The service uses river gauge information along with sample data to predict floods and provide alerts. As a general baseline, Google Flood Hub has been selected as it covers many areas of flood risk. However, it does not provide any device-level blocking detection, nor does it allow community members to directly report flooding.

### **2.2.2 Feature Comparison**

| Feature | Google Flood Hub | DrainWatch |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Flood forecasting | Yes | No |
| Water-level monitoring | Uses river gauges and sample data | Two sensors at different levels |
| Localized flood warning | Where coverage is available | Warning levels are notifications and threat levels use an alarm |
| Drain blockage reports | Not used as core feature | Residents are able to make reports |
| Real-time cameras to monitor high-risk zones | Nothing related | Proposed idea (new feature), use cameras to monitor certain water levels |
| Heat maps | Flood-risk maps | Heat maps to locate large areas with high water density |
| Emergency maintenance reporting | Nothing related | Proposed idea, actively report to authorities and maintenance teams |
| Community points system | Nothing related | Exchange points accumulated from valid reports for certain rewards |

 

 

### **2.2.3 Feature Comparison**

Advantages of using DrainWatch over existing models such as Google Flood Hub

* **Early Detection:** Drain sensors are directly installed in the drains within a municipality, allowing early detection of rising waters.  
* **2 Stage Response:** There is a 2 Stage response within the system. Within the first stage, users will be notified of a potential issue. If the issue worsens, it will then become a danger alert, which requires a physical evacuation of people.  
* **Community Driven:** Users can report issues. Users are rewarded based on a points system depending on whether their reports were accurate. This means that local authorities have less time spent manually checking for issues.  
* **Camera Monitoring in Risk Areas**: High-risk areas of water build-up are monitored with cameras.  
* **Heatmap:** A high-density heatmap of water levels is created to allow prioritisation of repairs in the most severely blocked areas.

### **2.2.4 Technology and Approaches Review**

The Google-based flood monitoring system uses software. DrainWatch however, uses local IoT hardware. The ESP32 is used as a cheap microcontroller. It allows processing of sensor data and connects to a Wi-Fi network. Detection of flooding threats is done using two mechanisms. Firstly, two float switches are placed at different heights. As the water level rises, these activate the two-stage alarm system. Secondly, a waterproof ultrasonic sensor is placed above the water. This is used as a backup mechanism. The readings from this sensor allow precise measurement of the height of water, which is needed to create heat maps. The entire system is housed within a waterproof case and is self-powered. A battery and small solar panel power it. Finally, there is a siren/buzzer, so that alarms can be raised in that location to cause evacuations.

## **3.3 System Analysis and Design Methodology**

### **3.3.1 Methodology Selection and Justification (OOADM / SSADM)**

DrainWatch is a civic technology project combining IoT hardware with an MQTT-based messaging layer, mobile application, and backend service. OOADM was selected because it applies consistently across all implementation layers, which are firmware (C++/Arduino via PlatformIO), messaging (MQTT broker), and application, all of which use object-oriented concepts. The following section compare OOADM and SSADM

| Perspective | OOADM | SSADM | Which one is better |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Core philosophy | Our project has natural objects such as sensors, users, drain alerts, reports, and cameras. Each of them maps directly to an object class, allowing the system to be modelled as interacting objects | It also has data flowing through processes. For example, data flows from the sensors to the alert system, then to notifications and residents, and reports that flow for validation and points awarding | Both methodologies can be used in our project, but OOADM's philosophy aligns better with our system requirements. |
| How it handle data Structure | Data stays inside classes as attributes. For example, the Sensor class encapsulates water level, battery, and location. | In SSADM, to handle data we use Logical Data Structure (LDS), Data Flow Diagram (DFD), and Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD). These focus on data movement and storage. | For our current development, OOADM is preferred because data and behaviour are tightly connected  to core components  |
| Suitability for event-driven / real-time systems | Handles events through objects communicating via messages. When a sensor triggers, the Alert object is created, which calls NotificationService, which notifies residents. | Focuses mainly on processing and storing data, making it less suitable for real-time event handling. | Our project's core function is real-time alert escalation, so OOADM is better here. |
| Documentation and learning curve | Documentation is lighter and integrated with the development process. UML diagrams are taught in OOP Module so most team members already have exposure to them. | Requires extensive documentation at each stage, including feasibility studies, investigation reports, and detailed analysis specifications. | OOADM is preferred for the current development phase, as the team is already familiar with UML Diagram   |
| Industry adoption Nowadays | Object-oriented approaches dominate modern commercial software development. | SSADM remains in use within government and public-sector IT contexts where DrainWatch's authority-side users operate. | OOADM is preferred, as it aligns with the project's modern toolchain and the team's industry-relevant skills. |

Note: While OOADM is selected as the primary methodology for DrainWatch's current development, SSADM may be considered for future development phases when the system scales to government deployment.

**Justification for choosing OOADM**   
Both OOADM and SSADM have their own advantages for our DrainWatch project, but we selected OOADM as the better methodology because it fits with the core parts of our system. DrainWatch is mainly an event-driven system, and its main features like the two-stage alert escalation, real-time sensor behaviour, and the plan to expand beyond drainage are all naturally object-oriented.

SSADM does have its strengths, especially in data modelling, documentation, and audit trails. These would be useful for our secondary parts like the reporting and points subsystems, where data management is the main concern. But these parts are not the core of our system. The core of DrainWatch is the alert state machine, sensor collaboration, and event-driven notification flow, which needs modelling techniques that SSADM does not provide directly. For example, we need state diagrams for the Normal → Warning → Threat → Evacuation transition, and sequence diagrams for object collaboration across our MQTT pub/sub architecture.

OOADM also fits well with our chosen technology stack. The ESP32 microcontroller will be programmed in C++ using Arduino IDE and PlatformIO, which are object-oriented environments. We are using two different sensor types (submersible water level sensor and JSN-SR04T ultrasonic sensor) with the same readLevel() interface, which is a good example of polymorphism. Our MQTT pub/sub architecture also maps directly onto OOADM's object collaboration model, where sensor objects publish readings to topics and alert manager objects subscribe and react. Also, our plan to expand DrainWatch beyond drainage into other civic maintenance areas works well with OOADM's extensibility through inheritance and polymorphism.

So we selected OOADM as the methodology for our DrainWatch project. We know that OOADM has some limitations, like performance overhead and the risk of tight coupling in inheritance designs like our User role hierarchy (Resident, Authority, MaintenanceWorker, Admin). But these can be managed with careful design practices. SSADM's assumptions about stable requirements and stage-gate completeness do not fit well with DrainWatch's plan to evolve and expand over time. However, we may consider SSADM for future development phases when DrainWatch scales to government deployment and needs more rigorous documentation and data structure management.   
![][image3]

### **3.3.1 Application of the Selected Methodology**

In Section 3.3.1, several methodologies were compared, and Agile OOADM (Object-Oriented Analysis and Design Methodology) was selected for the DrainWatch project. This section explains how the selected methodology will be applied to our work, and it presents the modelling techniques and the diagrams that we use to support system analysis and design. Bennett et al. (2010) describe OOADM as an approach that treats a system as a collection of cooperating objects and produces models of these objects in a step-by-step manner. DrainWatch consists of natural objects such as sensors, alarms, applications and reports; therefore, OOADM provides a clear path from our requirements to our implementation.

Agile working adds the iterative dimension. The system is developed in short sprints, and each sprint ends with a small working part of DrainWatch that can be tested and demonstrated. The methodology therefore provides both the structure of the models and the rhythm of the development process. The models themselves are presented in the design chapter (Chapter 6); this section explains how the methodology leads to each of them.

**Application of Agile OOADM across the Project Lifecycle**

Agile OOADM is applied as a repeating cycle of four stages: analysis, design, implementation and testing. Each sprint begins with a small set of requirements and passes through all four stages, which keeps the models in close alignment with the working code.

At the beginning of a sprint, requirements are collected. Our citizen survey established the main needs of residents, and these needs are converted into user stories for the sprint. The team then moves into analysis, where the user stories are examined to identify the actors and the data flows they contain. These are modelled with a use case diagram and a data flow diagram, which allow the team to agree on what the system must do and where every reading must travel.

Analysis is followed by design, in which technical decisions are added to the analysis models: how the ESP32 will make decisions at the edge, which MQTT topics the messages will use, how the backend will store and forward the readings, and what the resident application and the council dashboard will receive. The order of the messages is captured in a sequence diagram, and the behaviour of the device is captured in an activity diagram. This stage also covers the design of the MQTT topics and the data store, connecting the models to the underlying technology.

The design is then implemented. The Arduino C++ program for the ESP32 sensor node, the Python code for the backend and the mobile application are written during this stage. All code is kept on GitHub, which allows the team members to work on different components in parallel. Each component is tested within every sprint: the device is first tested in the Wokwi simulator, because simulation is low-risk and cost-effective, and the backend is tested against the simulated device before real hardware is used.

At the end of every sprint, the working part of the system is demonstrated to the supervisor, feedback is collected, and the next sprint is planned. Consequently, when requirements change — for example, when a new idea emerges from the survey — the change is added as a new user story in the following sprint. Agile working absorbs this change, and the object-oriented structure keeps it small, since usually only one component needs to be modified rather than the whole system.

**Modelling Techniques**

The selected methodology provides a compact set of modelling techniques, and each technique presents one view of DrainWatch. Use case modelling captures the functional requirements from the point of view of the actors. Data flow modelling represents how the water level readings travel through the system, from the sensors to the alarms and the applications; this technique was chosen because DrainWatch is fundamentally a data pipeline. Interaction modelling represents the movement of messages between the devices over time and is expressed through a sequence diagram. Activity modelling represents the workflow inside the device, including its decisions, branches and loops. All models are drawn in draw.io, so they can be updated quickly at the end of each sprint.

**Diagrams Supporting Analysis and Design**

| Diagram | Modelling Technique  | Supports | Purpose for DrainWatch |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Use case Diagram |  |  |  |
| Data flow Diagram | Data flow Modelling | Analysis and Design | The journey of a reading: sensors, ESP32, backend, data store, resident application and council dashboard |
| Sequence Diagram | Interaction modelling | Design | The message order of a flood warning across the six components of the system |
| Activity Diagram | Activity modelling | Design | The start-up and running workflow of the device, including its decisions and loops |

**Use case diagram**:

**Data flow diagram**: The data flow diagram traces the journey of a single reading through DrainWatch. The ultrasonic sensor and the water level sensor send their level data to process 1, Read and decide, which executes on the ESP32. This process performs the edge decision and sends a trigger directly to the wide-area alarm, so the local siren operates even when the internet connection is unavailable. The same process publishes the reading or the alert over MQTT to process 2, Process and store, which executes on the backend. The backend writes the readings into data store D1, pushes notifications to the resident application, and displays the status on the council dashboard. The diagram therefore defined the two-process architecture, the data store and the recipients of each output, and it directly informed the design of the MQTT topics.

**Sequence diagram**: The sequence diagram represents the same warning flow as messages over time, with six lifelines: Device Sensors, ESP32, MQTT broker, Backend, Council dashboard and Resident app. The sensors read the level and return the water level reading to the ESP32. The ESP32 compares the reading with the warning threshold, and when the level reaches it, the device sets its state to WARNING. The ESP32 then publishes the alert to the MQTT broker, the broker delivers it to the backend, and the backend stores the reading. The backend subsequently displays the warning on the council dashboard and pushes the notification to the resident application. As a design model, the diagram fixes the exact order of the messages that the implementation must send and receive.

**Activity diagram**: The activity diagram represents the workflow inside the device, from start-up to the running loop. It begins when the module is inserted, the battery is connected and the connection is confirmed. A decision then checks the battery reading, and when the battery reads 100 per cent, the device sets its state to FULL and decodes the data. A second decision on the start mode directs the flow into three paths: in Running, the device publishes the WARNING alert; in Normal, it joins the network, connects Wi-Fi and shuts down; and in Timeout, it creates a reference alert and publishes the evaluation alert. Finally, the timed commands execute in a loop, and the END LOOP returns the flow to the start. The diagram supports the design because it constitutes a direct plan for the Arduino code, with every decision and loop represented in a single view.

**Integration of the Models**

Together, these diagrams form one connected model of DrainWatch. The use cases state what the system must do, the data flow diagram states where the readings travel, the sequence diagram states the order in which the messages move, and the activity diagram states how the device behaves internally. All diagrams are maintained in draw.io and updated at the end of every sprint, so the documentation remains consistent with the working code.The models also support communication within the team, since all members can examine the same flows before implementation begins; they are presented individually in the design chapter (chapter 6).

## **4.2 Stakeholder Analysis**

Stakeholders can be divided into 4 groups depending upon their relationship to DrainWatch using an Onion Model.

**Ring 1**

**DrainWatch**

This system gathers reports of obstructions in drainage systems, provides information on drainage conditions, floods and updates on maintenance.

**Ring 2**

**Resident**

Users of DrainWatch. They submit reports of blockages and receive flood warnings specific to their area.

**Maintenance Staff**

Staff within the field. They receive alerts to go out and complete maintenance, and update the status of whether blockages have been solved.

**Programmers**

Staff within the team who program, upload, update and maintain DrainWatch.

**Technicians**

Staff within the hardware/field team. They install, configure and maintain the DrainWatch sensors.

**Ring 3:** **Owners, Beneficiaries and Experts**

 **Local Council (Owner)**

Owner of DrainWatch. They are responsible for funding DrainWatch, and working with other agencies.

**Emergency Services**

Firefighters, rescue services and disaster management. Work with the Local Council in extreme flooding events.

**Engineers/Experts**

Civil, Hydraulic and Drainage engineers. Provide expert advice to the Local Council regarding optimal design and reducing flooding risks.

**Ring 4: Externals / Negative Stakeholders**

**Government**

National or regional government. They provide policy guidelines, legal requirements and funding to infrastructures within the Local Council.

**Regulatory Bodies**

Responsible for ensuring that the Local Council and DrainWatch operate appropriately within environmental, safety, city and data protection regulations.

**Insurance companies**

Use knowledge of flooding within the Local Council to assess the risk to properties, and reduce flood claims.

**ISPs (Internet Service Providers)**

Provide internet connections for DrainWatch server, mobile users and sensors.

**Maps API**

External companies providing maps, markers, and route information within DrainWatch.

**Competition (Negative Stakeholder)**

Other companies like Google within Smart City Monitoring/Drainage Monitoring. Competing with DrainWatch for contracts/budgets with the Local Council.

**Atackers (Negative Stakeholder)**

Hackers looking to damage DrainWatch through hacking, corrupting data, disrupting services and interference with devices.

# **Chapter 5: Social, Legal, Ethical and Professional Issues**

## **5.1 Chapter Overview**

Building DrainWatch involved more than writing code and connecting sensors. Because our system deals with public safety, personal data and community trust, a number of wider issues had to be considered alongside the technical work. DrainWatch issues emergency alerts that influence how people respond during a flood, collects personal data through user accounts and blockage reports, operates cameras in public spaces, and manages a points system that rewards verified reports. Each of these raises questions about what is right, what is lawful, and what our responsibilities are as developers. This chapter therefore examines the social, legal, ethical and professional (SLEP) issues arising from our project, together with the related areas of security, equality and sustainability. These issues emerged through our citizen survey, in which respondents raised privacy concerns, through our comparison with Google Flood Hub, and through design decisions taken during development, such as the inclusion of cameras and the points system. The chapter first describes the ethical review process we followed, then discusses each of the six SLEP areas in turn, before summarizing the key risks and how we addressed them in a concluding table.

## **5.2 Ethical Clearance**

## **5.3 SLEP Issues and Mitigation**

In this section we discuss the six SLEP areas one by one. For every area we first explain the issue for DrainWatch, and then we explain our mitigation, in other words how we reduce the risk. The areas are legal issues, ethical issues, security, equality, diversity and inclusion, sustainability and professional issues. At the end of the section, Table 5.1 brings all the risks and mitigations together in one view 

**Legal Issues**

Our system stores personal data, so data protection is our biggest legal area. We follow the UK GDPR principles, and because DrainWatch will work in Sri Lanka, we also follow the Personal Data Protection Act No. 9 of 2022\. Both laws ask for the same core duties: collect data fairly and openly, use it only for the stated purpose, keep it safe, and delete it when the purpose ends.

So we designed DrainWatch to collect as little data as possible. A resident can send a report with only a photo and a GPS location, and a name is optional. The backend keeps reports only while the Authority needs them for verification, and old reports are deleted after that. We also separate the roles in the system, so a Resident cannot open another person's data, and only the Authority can see the full report queue. If a data breach ever happens, we will inform our supervisor and the local authority straight away, as the laws require.

Intellectual property is our second legal area. Our team writes all the DrainWatch code ourselves, and we keep it in a private GitHub repository while the project runs. We use open-source libraries, for example the MQTT library for our ESP32 code and Python libraries for our backend. Before we publish anything, we will check every library licence, such as MIT or Apache 2.0, and we will credit the authors in our repository. We will also add a licence file for our own code, so other people know what they may do with it. Also, we will not use copied images, icons or sounds without permission, because that would break copyright**.**

**Ethical Issues**

Privacy is the biggest ethical risk in DrainWatch. Our camera watches a public drain, so people who never agreed to our project can walk past it. Our reports also carry GPS locations, which can show where a person lives. So we made three design decisions. The camera only watches the drain, and a sign near it tells people that recording happens. We do not use face recognition, and we blur faces in stored footage. And the heat map only shows zone levels, never individual reports, so nobody can trace a report back to one house.

Consent matters in every place where a person joins the system. Survey participants tick a consent box before they answer. Report submitters see a short message that their photo and location will be shared with the Authority, so they decide with open eyes. Also, we never use the reward points as unfair pressure: a resident who does not want to send reports can still use the warnings and the heat map for free.

Bias is a quieter ethical risk. If we listen only to smartphone users, the areas with fewer smartphone owners would look safer than they really are. So our heat map combines sensor readings with community reports, and our survey was trilingual, in Sinhala, Tamil and English, so language does not decide who is heard. We also thought about the needs of others. Elderly residents and people without smartphones still get full protection, because the buzzer alarms on the sensor nodes work without any mobile application.

**Security Issues**

Security is built into our design from the first sprint, not added at the end. Our sensor nodes talk over MQTT, so the broker asks for a username and password on every connection, and every node has its own credentials. The backend checks every message before it stores it, so a broken or fake reading cannot reach the database or the alarms.

On the application side, passwords are stored as hashes and never as plain text. The photo upload checks the file size and the file type, so a user cannot send a harmful file instead of a picture. Every role gets the smallest rights it needs: Residents create and see their own reports, the Authority verifies the reports, and the Admin manages the users.

Also, security is part of every iteration. At the end of each sprint we test the new feature with normal inputs and with wrong inputs, for example an empty report or a very large file, before we mark the sprint as done. When we find a weakness, we fix it in the same sprint, or we write it as a task for the next sprint. So security grows together with the system instead of chasing it.

**Equality, Diversity and Inclusion**

Sri Lanka has three main languages, so an English-only system would exclude many people. From the start we made our citizen survey trilingual, in Sinhala, Tamil and English, and we plan the mobile application in the same three languages. The application will use simple sentences and clear icons, so residents with low literacy can still use it with confidence.

Accessibility also means more than language. Our alarms do not depend on colour alone: the mobile warning shows colour and text together, and the node buzzer gives a sound signal, so a colour-blind or visually impaired resident is not left out. The application stays light, so it also works on cheap and older phones. And DrainWatch is free for residents, so income does not decide who gets protection. These choices follow the public interest duty in the BCS Code of Conduct, which asks us to make technology that works for everyone 

**Sustainability**

We thought about the environmental impact of our hardware. Each sensor node runs on a rechargeable 18650 battery charged by a small solar panel, so we do not throw away single-use batteries every few weeks. The ESP32 sleeps between readings to save power, and the IP67 enclosure protects the electronics from water and dust, so a node lasts for years and we replace fewer parts. At the end of its life, the standard parts inside a node, such as the battery and the board, can be recycled separately.

The bigger sustainability story is social. DrainWatch helps a community to see flood risks early, and blocked drains get cleared before they cause damage, so the system supports a safer neighbourhood for many years. The points and rewards keep residents engaged even after our project team leaves, because the community itself continues to report and verify. So our environmental footprint stays small, and the social value keeps growing.

**Professional Issues**

As future computing professionals we follow the BCS Code of Conduct. The code asks us to work for the public interest, and DrainWatch is a public safety system, so this duty guides our design choices, for example the privacy protections in section 5.3.2. The code asks us to work within the law, and that is why we follow the UK GDPR and the Sri Lankan data protection act in this project. The code also asks us to work within our competence: we only take tasks we can do or learn with help, and we ask our supervisor when we are unsure.

Professional behaviour also shapes how our team works. We split the tasks fairly between the five of us, we review each other's code on GitHub politely, and we tell the team early when a task is late, so nobody hides a problem. Towards our supervisor and the local authority we stay honest: we show real results, we admit what does not work yet, and we never promise a feature that we cannot deliver. So our behaviour inside the team and outside it follows the same professional standard.

**Table Here**

## **5.4 Chapter Summary**

In this chapter we looked at DrainWatch through a wider lens than code. We showed our ethical clearance first: we completed the UoW Form A process before our survey, we protected our participants with anonymity and consent, and we declared that we use no external dataset. Then we discussed the six SLEP areas, and we gave a mitigation for every issue.

The main lessons for us are three. First, privacy shapes our whole design, from the camera sign to the zone-level heat map, because photos and GPS locations are personal data. Second, security only works when it is built into every sprint, so we test each new feature with wrong inputs as well as normal ones. Third, the BCS Code of Conduct gives us a practical checklist for our behaviour inside the team and towards the community. With these duties in place, we believe DrainWatch is not only a working system but also a responsible one
